questions.title: How is Hyperspherical Energy formally defined and why does it specifically use the sum of inverse distances?
questions.question_body: I am struggling to comprehend the mathematical definition of Hyperspherical Energy (HE) provided in Equation 1: $\text{HE}(\bm{W}):= \sum_{i\neq j} \|\hat{\bm{w}}_i-\hat{\bm{w}}_j\|^{-1}$. The paper states that HE captures the 'level of neuron uniformity on the unit hypersphere,' but I don't intuitively understand why summing the inverse Euclidean distances between normalized neurons quantifies this. If all neurons point in exactly the same direction, does this metric go to infinity? Conversely, if they are perfectly uniformly distributed (maximally separated), does it approach a specific minimum? I need a concrete derivation showing how this formula relates to geometric uniformity on a sphere.

questions.title: What is the precise relationship between preserving pairwise angles and preserving Hyperspherical Energy?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that OFT 'provably preserves hyperspherical energy' by applying an orthogonal transformation. In Section 2.1, it states that $\min \| \text{HE}(\bm{W})-\text{HE}(\bm{W}^0) \|=0$ is achieved if $\bm{W}=\bm{R}\bm{W}^0$ where $\bm{R}$ is orthogonal. Given that hyperspherical energy depends only on the norms of differences between normalized vectors ($\| \hat{w}_i - \hat{w}_j \\|$), and normalized vectors depend only on angles (since magnitude is 1), could someone explain step-by-step why rotating *all* neurons by an orthogonal matrix leaves these pairwise distances unchanged? Does this hold true even if the rotation changes the absolute coordinates significantly?

questions.title: Why does Constrained Orthogonal Finetuning (COFT) require a projection step on $\\bm{Q}$ but OFT does not?
questions.question_body: I have a detailed question regarding the implementation of COFT vs standard OFT. The paper introduces COFT with the constraint $\\|\\bm{R}-\\bm{I}\\|\\leq \\epsilon$. It mentions using Cayley parameterization ($\\bm{R}=(\\bm{I}+\\bm{Q})(\\mathbf{I}-\\bm{Q})^{-1}$) and then projecting a constraint onto $\\bm{Q}$ using Neumann series approximation ($\\|\\mathbf{{{Q}}}-\\mathbf{{{0}}}||||leq \\epsilon'$). However, standard OFT only enforces orthogonality ($\\constexpr R^	op R = I$). Why isn't there an explicit upper bound on the distance from identity in standard OFT? If OFT allows $R$ to be any orthogonal matrix (including one far from identity), doesn't that violate the goal of preserving pretrained semantics better than implicitly assuming small changes?

questions.title: How does OFT handle layers with different input/output dimensions compared to block-diagonal decomposition?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.2, the authors discuss parameter efficiency using a block-diagonal matrix $R`=`diag(R_1, ..., R_r)` where each block is `O(d/r). However, standard diffusion models often have layers with mismatched dimensions (e.g., Convolution layers or Attention mechanisms where Query/Key/Value dimensions differ). If `d` represents feature dimension and `n` represents number of channels/neurons, how exactly do we construct an orthogonal matrix `R` when applying OFT to a Transformer's attention weight matrix which might be `d_q x d_k` or applied to multiple head dimensions simultaneously? Does the block size depend on `d` or `n`, and what happens if `d` cannot be evenly divided by `r`?

questions.title: Is there a theoretical connection between OFT's preservation of global structure and LoRA's low-rank adaptation regarding information collapse?
questions.question_body: The paper contrasts OFT with LoRA by saying LoRA prevents 'information shifting dramatically' via low-rank constraints, while OFT prevents 'destroying pretraining information' via orthogonality. I am curious about the theoretical implications here. If LoRA updates are restricted to rank `r', they inherently discard information orthogonal to those subspace directions. Does OFT technically preserve *more* information theoretically because an orthogonal transformation (full rank) preserves all existing variance in the weight space? If so, why doesn't this lead to overfitting differently from LoRA? Also, since OFT learns `R`, isn't there still a risk that `R - I` becomes full rank locally during training, effectively changing everything despite the global orthogonality constraint?
